analogy.p: Magnetic storage is like a giant filing cabinet with a clerk who runs to the right drawer: it holds a huge amount cheaply but takes a moment and can be damaged if shaken. Optical storage is like a printed book you read with a torch: cheap to copy and light to post, but small and easily scratched. Solid state is like a whiteboard that you read and rewrite instantly with no moving parts, tough and quick, but costing more per metre of board. The analogy breaks down because real storage holds data as magnetised areas, pits and lands or trapped charge, not as written words, and flash cells eventually wear out whereas a whiteboard does not.

bullets: Know the **need for secondary storage** and why it is **non-volatile**.
Know the three types: **magnetic**, **optical** and **solid state**, with examples of each.
Know the **characteristics**: capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability, cost.
Be able to **choose a suitable device or medium** for a scenario and justify it.
Be able to state **advantages and disadvantages** of each type.
Know the basic idea of **how each type stores data** (magnetised areas, pits and lands, trapped charge).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 1.2 requires you to know why computers need secondary storage, the three common types (magnetic, optical and solid state), and how to judge a device using the characteristics of capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost. You must be able to choose a suitable storage device or medium for a given application and justify the choice, and to state the advantages and disadvantages of each type. This is tested as 1 to 2 mark recall, 4 mark compare questions and 6 mark recommend or discuss questions.

bullets: Secondary storage is **non-volatile**: data is **kept when the power is off**.
It has a **much larger capacity** than RAM (hundreds of GB to several TB).
It is **cheaper per GB** than RAM, so it is the practical place for **long-term storage**.
It stores the **operating system, applications, documents, photos and music**.
It is **not directly accessed by the CPU**: data is **copied into RAM** first.
It is **slower** than RAM, which is why it cannot replace RAM.
Link: the same device can also be used for **virtual memory** (previous topic).
core.p: Primary storage such as RAM is volatile, so everything in it is lost when the power is turned off, and RAM is also too small and expensive to hold all the programs and files a user owns. Secondary storage is therefore needed to keep the operating system, programs and files permanently, even when the computer is switched off. It is non-volatile, much larger and cheaper per gigabyte than RAM, but slower, and the CPU cannot access it directly, so data must be loaded into RAM before it is used.

bullets: **Capacity**: how much data the device can store (measured in bytes, such as GB or TB).
**Speed**: how quickly data can be read from and written to the device (access and transfer speed).
**Portability**: how easy it is to carry around; related to **size and weight**.
**Durability**: how well it survives being dropped, scratched, heated or knocked (moving parts reduce this).
**Reliability**: how long and how consistently it works without failing or losing data.
**Cost**: the price, often compared as **cost per GB**.
Always **link the characteristic to the scenario**: 'it is durable, so it will survive being carried in a rucksack'.
core.h: The six characteristics used to compare storage
core.p: Exam questions almost always ask you to choose or compare using named characteristics, so you must be able to define each one and apply it. Choosing the best device is about matching the characteristics to the needs of the user: a photographer wants a lot of capacity in a portable form, whereas a company archive wants cheap, reliable storage for a huge amount of data. Always link a characteristic to the scenario rather than just stating it.

bullets: Data is stored as **magnetised areas** (one of two magnetic states, representing **1 or 0**).
An HDD has **spinning platters**, a **read/write head** and an **actuator arm**.
The platters spin quickly, and the arm **moves the head** to the right track to find data.
The moving parts mean there is a **delay** while the head and platter get into position.
Examples: **hard disk drive (internal or external)** and **magnetic tape**.
**Magnetic tape** stores data on a long reel of tape and is accessed **in sequence**, so it is slow to find one file.
Tape has **very large capacity and is cheap**, so it is used for **backups and archives**.
core.p: Magnetic storage records data as patterns of magnetism on a surface. In a hard disk drive (HDD), the data is stored on one or more rapidly spinning metal platters coated with a magnetic material. Tiny areas of the platter are magnetised in one direction or the other to represent 1s and 0s. A read/write head on a moving arm hovers very close to the surface and either detects the magnetised pattern to read data or changes it to write data.

bullets: **Advantage**: **large capacity** (many terabytes).
**Advantage**: **low cost per GB**, the cheapest of the common types for large amounts of data.
**Advantage**: a long track record and **reasonably reliable** if treated carefully.
**Disadvantage**: **moving parts**, so they are **less durable** and can be damaged by knocks or drops.
**Disadvantage**: **slower** than solid state because the head and platter must move.
**Disadvantage**: **heavier, noisier and use more power** than solid state, producing heat.
**Disadvantage**: a spinning disk is **less portable**; external drives are portable but fragile.
core.p: Magnetic hard disk drives give by far the best capacity for the price, which makes them the standard choice for storing large amounts of data cheaply, for example in desktop computers, servers and external backup drives. However, their moving parts make them slower than solid state, noisier, heavier, more power hungry and more easily damaged by knocks, especially when spinning. They are therefore less suitable for portable devices that are often moved or dropped.

bullets: Data is stored as a **spiral track** of **pits and lands** on the disc surface.
A **laser** is shone at the disc and the **reflection is detected** by a sensor.
**Lands** reflect the light; **pits** scatter it, so the sensor sees **different reflections** representing 1s and 0s.
Examples: **CD, DVD, Blu-ray**.
Typical single-layer capacities: **CD about 700 MB**, **DVD about 4.7 GB**, **Blu-ray about 25 GB**.
Types: **ROM** (pre-pressed, read only), **R** (record once) and **RW** (rewritable).
Blu-ray uses a **shorter wavelength laser**, so its pits are smaller and more data fits on the disc.
core.p: Optical storage uses a laser to read data from a disc. The surface of the disc has a long spiral track containing tiny dents called pits and flat areas called lands. A laser shines on the track and a sensor detects how the light is reflected: lands reflect the light strongly while pits scatter it, and the changes between the two are interpreted as 1s and 0s. In writable discs, the laser is used to burn or alter marks on the disc to create the pattern.

bullets: **Advantage**: **very cheap** per disc and cheap to mass-produce.
**Advantage**: **portable** (thin and light) and easy to post.
**Advantage**: **read-only discs cannot be accidentally overwritten**, which suits distributing films or software.
**Disadvantage**: **low capacity** compared with HDDs and SSDs.
**Disadvantage**: **slower** read and write speeds.
**Disadvantage**: **scratches and damage** easily, so **low durability**; discs can also warp or degrade over time.
**Disadvantage**: needs an **optical drive**, which many new laptops do not have.
core.p: Optical discs are cheap to produce, light and easy to post, so they are well suited to distributing films, music and software in large numbers, and to cheap, one-off backups. Their disadvantages are a low capacity compared with modern hard drives or flash storage, slower access speeds, and the fact that the surface scratches or degrades, so they are not durable. Many modern computers no longer include an optical drive for these reasons.

bullets: Uses **flash memory** built from **transistors**, with **no moving parts**.
Data is stored by **trapping electrical charge** in cells, representing **1 or 0**.
Data is read and written **electronically**, which is why it is **very fast**.
Examples: **solid state drive (SSD)**, **USB flash drive**, **SD card**, phone storage.
The data is **non-volatile**: it remains after power is removed.
Each cell can only be **written a limited number of times** before it wears out, though this is rarely a problem in normal use.
Because there are no moving parts, SSDs are **silent**, **lighter** and **use less power**.
core.h: Solid state storage: how it works
core.p: Solid state storage has no moving parts. It uses flash memory, which is made of electronic circuits (transistors) arranged in a grid of cells. Each cell can trap an electrical charge or not, and whether a charge is present represents a 1 or a 0. Because data is read and written electronically, access is very quick, and because the charge stays trapped without power, the memory is non-volatile.

bullets: **Advantage**: **no moving parts**, so very **durable** and resistant to knocks and vibration.
**Advantage**: **very fast** access and data transfer, so programs open and computers boot quickly.
**Advantage**: **silent, light and low power**, so ideal for **portable devices** and longer battery life.
**Advantage**: **small and portable** (USB sticks, SD cards).
**Disadvantage**: **more expensive per GB** than magnetic storage.
**Disadvantage**: **lower capacity for the same price**, and very large SSDs are costly.
**Disadvantage**: **limited number of write cycles** per cell, so it can wear out over a long time.
core.h: Solid state storage: advantages and disadvantages
core.p: Solid state storage has become the standard in laptops, tablets, phones and cameras because it is fast, durable, silent and light. It is more expensive per gigabyte than magnetic storage and is usually sold in smaller capacities for the same price, and flash cells have a limited number of write cycles. When a question needs a portable, durable, fast device that is quiet and low power, solid state is usually the answer; when the need is for cheap, huge capacity, magnetic is usually better.

bullets: **Capacity**: magnetic is **highest** (TBs), solid state is **medium to high**, optical is **lowest**.
**Speed**: solid state is **fastest**, magnetic is **medium**, optical is **slowest**.
**Portability**: **optical and solid state** are very portable; internal **magnetic** drives are not.
**Durability**: **solid state** is best (no moving parts); magnetic and optical are more easily damaged.
**Cost per GB**: **magnetic** is cheapest for large capacity; optical is cheap per disc; solid state is more expensive per GB.
**Power use**: solid state uses least; magnetic uses more because of the spinning disk.
Always use **comparative words** such as 'faster', 'more durable', 'cheaper per GB'.
core.p: A good answer to a comparison question refers to the same characteristic for each type, so it is helpful to memorise a mental table. Magnetic storage is large, cheap, fairly slow and fragile; optical is cheap and portable but small, slow and easily scratched; solid state is fast, durable, portable and low power but more expensive for large amounts. These are typical relationships rather than exact figures, but they are exactly what mark schemes expect.

bullets: **Smartphone / tablet / camera**: **solid state** (flash or SD card) because it is **small, light, durable, fast and low power**.
**Laptop**: often an **SSD** for **speed, durability and battery life**.
**Large archive or backup of lots of data**: **magnetic** (external hard drive or tape) for **large capacity at low cost per GB**.
**Distributing films, music or software**: **optical** (DVD/Blu-ray) because discs are **cheap and light to produce and post**.
**Portable transfer of files between computers**: a **USB flash drive** because it is **small, durable and plug-and-play**.
**Server holding large amounts of frequently used data**: SSDs for speed or HDDs for cost, depending on the need.
Structure: **need, device, reason (linked to characteristics)**.
core.h: Choosing a device for an application
core.p: When you are asked to recommend storage, identify the key needs in the scenario, state the best type, name a specific device, and justify it with at least two characteristics. The reasons are what earn the marks, so a bare device name earns little. Avoid choosing something that conflicts with the scenario, for example a fragile, heavy magnetic drive for a device that will be carried around a lot.

bullets: **Units**: capacity is measured in bytes, KB, MB, GB, TB, with each step 1000 times bigger in the OCR spec.
**Compression** reduces file size so more files fit on the same storage.
**Cloud storage** keeps data on remote servers accessed over the internet, an alternative to local devices.
Secondary storage holds **virtual memory**, which is why an SSD makes virtual memory less slow than an HDD.
**Backups** use secondary storage to protect against data loss.
**Embedded systems** often use flash memory for their stored program or settings.
**Environmental/ethical link**: SSDs use less power, but discs and drives must be recycled properly.
core.h: Links to other topics and extension ideas
core.p: Secondary storage connects to many other parts of the course. It is where data is stored after being created, which links to units of capacity (bytes, KB, MB, GB, TB) and to file size calculations in the next spec point. It links to compression, because files are compressed to take up less space, and to cloud storage, which stores data on remote servers instead of local devices. Understanding these links helps you in 6 mark discuss questions.

bullets: **1 byte = 8 bits**; 1 kB = 1000 bytes; 1 MB = 1000 kB; 1 GB = 1000 MB; 1 TB = 1000 GB; 1 PB = 1000 TB.
Number of files that fit = **device capacity ÷ file size** (convert to the same unit first).
Example: a 32 GB card and 4 MB photos: 32 GB = 32 000 MB, and 32 000 ÷ 4 = **8000 photos**.
Total storage needed = number of files × size of each file.
Optical discs are small in capacity (CD about 700 MB, DVD about 4.7 GB, Blu-ray about 25 GB per layer).
Hard disk drives and SSDs are quoted in **GB and TB**; tape archives can hold even more.
Compression reduces file size so more files fit on the same device.
Check your answer is sensible: a phone holding millions of photos would be a sign of a unit error.
core.p: Secondary storage is measured in bytes, and OCR expects you to know the units from bit up to petabyte, with each unit 1000 times bigger than the one before. A bit is a single 1 or 0, a nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8 bits, then kilobyte (kB), megabyte (MB), gigabyte (GB), terabyte (TB) and petabyte (PB). These units let you judge whether a device is big enough for a task, for example whether a memory card can hold a number of photos. Always convert to the same unit before comparing or dividing, and show the working so method marks are not lost.

bullets: Naming: magnetic = hard disk drive or tape; optical = CD, DVD, Blu-ray; solid state = SSD, USB stick, SD card.
How data is stored: **magnetised areas** (magnetic), **pits and lands read by a laser** (optical), **trapped charge in flash cells** (solid state).
Explain *why* a property follows: SSDs are fast **because there are no moving parts**, so nothing has to spin or move into position.
Link every advantage to the scenario given, for example 'portable, so it fits in a pocket'.
Do not confuse **secondary storage** with **RAM**; RAM is volatile and directly accessed by the CPU.
For 'compare' questions, mention both devices and use the same characteristic for each.
Use the mark scheme words: capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability, cost.
Avoid brand names as the only answer; name the **type** of storage first.
core.p: Storage questions on Paper 1 usually come in three styles: a one-mark naming question, a two or three mark 'describe how data is stored' question, and a four to six mark recommendation or comparison. For the longer ones, plan before writing: pick the device, then give at least two reasons each linked to a characteristic and to the scenario. Use comparative words such as 'faster than', 'cheaper per GB' and 'more durable because it has no moving parts', and avoid vague answers such as 'it is better' or 'it has more memory'. Always say which type of storage you mean, and give a named device as an example.

exam: **State the type / give an example** (1 mark): 'magnetic: hard disk drive', 'optical: DVD', 'solid state: SSD' are all safe, specific answers.
**Describe how data is stored** (2 marks): magnetic = areas magnetised in two directions; optical = pits and lands read by a laser; solid state = charge trapped in flash memory cells.
**Give one advantage and one disadvantage** (2 marks): use characteristics, for example 'SSD is faster (1)' and 'SSD is more expensive per GB (1)'.
**Compare** (4 marks): use comparative words and cover the same characteristic for both, such as 'an SSD is faster than an HDD because it has no moving parts'.
**Choose a suitable device** (2 to 3 marks): name the device (1) and give a reason linked to the scenario (1 or 2).

**6 mark recommend / discuss**: consider several characteristics (capacity, speed, portability, durability, cost), refer to the scenario, weigh up advantages and disadvantages, then give a justified conclusion.
**Why is secondary storage needed?** (2 marks): RAM is volatile (1) and secondary storage keeps data when the power is off / holds files permanently (1).
Do **not** write 'it is cheaper' without 'per GB' or 'than ...'; examiners want a **comparison**.
Avoid vague words like 'good', 'better' or 'modern'. Use **durable, portable, high capacity, faster, cheaper per GB**.
Write the **brand-neutral device**: 'external hard drive', 'SD card', 'USB flash drive', not a product name.
For tape, mention **backup/archive** and **sequential access** to earn marks.
**Calculate how many files fit** (2 marks): convert units (GB to MB), then divide capacity by file size; for example 32 GB ÷ 4 MB = 8000 files.

mistakes.r: SSDs are faster because they have no moving parts and data is read and written electronically.
mistakes.w: SSDs are faster because they have lots of memory.

mistakes.r: Optical discs store data as pits and lands read by a laser.
mistakes.w: Optical discs store data using magnets.

mistakes.r: Solid state uses flash memory (trapped electrical charge) and has no moving parts.
Link a characteristic to the scenario: 'durable so it survives being dropped'.
mistakes.w: It is better because it is good.

mistakes.r: HDDs are slower than SSDs because the platter and head must move.
Secondary storage is non-volatile, larger and slower, and not directly accessed by the CPU.
mistakes.w: Secondary storage is the same as RAM.

mistakes.r: They are cheap but low capacity, slow and easily scratched; choose them only when suited, for example distributing films.
mistakes.w: Optical discs are the best because they are cheap, so use them for everything.

mistakes.r: Magnetic tape is accessed in sequence, so finding one file can be slow; it suits backups.
mistakes.w: Tape is quick to find a file.

mistakes.r: A USB flash drive is solid state (flash memory).
A hard disk drive stores data as magnetised areas on spinning platters read by a head on an actuator arm.
mistakes.w: A hard disk drive stores data on a laser-read disc or in flash chips.

summary: OCR J277 1.2 asks you to explain why secondary storage is needed, to describe how magnetic, optical and solid state storage work, and to compare them using capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost so you can recommend a device for an application. Choosing and justifying storage devices is a regular 4 to 6 mark question on Paper 1.

terms.d: Non-volatile, long-term storage that is not directly accessed by the CPU.
Keeps its contents when the power is turned off.
Storage that uses magnetised areas on a surface to represent data, such as a hard disk drive or magnetic tape.
A magnetic storage device with spinning platters and a read/write head on a moving arm.
Magnetic storage on a long reel of tape, accessed in sequence, used for backups and archives.
Storage in which a laser reads (and writes) pits and lands on a disc, such as CD, DVD and Blu-ray.
Pits are tiny dents and lands are flat areas on an optical disc; they reflect laser light differently to represent 1s and 0s.
Storage with no moving parts that uses flash memory (trapped electrical charge) to store data, such as an SSD or USB stick.
Non-volatile electronic memory that can be erased and rewritten and has no moving parts.
Solid state drive: a storage device made from flash memory.
The amount of data a storage device can hold.
How easy it is to carry or move the device.
How well a device withstands knocks, scratches and wear.
How consistently a device works without failure or data loss.
The price of a storage device divided by how much it can store.
A circular disc coated with magnetic material inside a hard disk drive that spins while data is read and written.
The part of a hard disk drive that reads and writes the magnetised areas on the platter.
A track is a ring of data on a disc; a sector is a section of a track.
The single track of pits and lands on an optical disc that the laser follows.

worked.ans: An SD card (solid state): durable, small and portable, with enough capacity and fast writing for thousands of photos.
worked.q: A photographer travels to remote places and takes thousands of photos. Recommend a suitable storage device and justify your choice. [4 marks]
steps: Device: SD card / solid state storage (1).
It is durable because it has no moving parts, so it survives being knocked or dropped on location (1).
It is small and light so it is portable (1).
It has enough capacity to store many photos and is fast to write, so photos can be saved quickly (1).

worked.ans: Magnetic: cheaper per GB and larger capacity but slower and less durable. Solid state: faster, more durable and lower power but more expensive per GB.
worked.q: Compare magnetic and solid state storage. [4 marks]
steps: Magnetic storage (HDD) has a larger capacity for the same price / cheaper per GB, whereas solid state costs more per GB (1 + 1).
Solid state is faster because it has no moving parts, whereas magnetic is slower because the head and platter must move (1 + 1).
Alternatively: solid state is more durable and uses less power; magnetic is more easily damaged.

worked.ans: Pits and lands on a spiral track are read by a laser: the reflection is detected and interpreted as 1s and 0s.
worked.q: Describe how data is stored and read on an optical disc. [3 marks]
steps: Data is stored as pits and lands on a spiral track (1).
A laser is shone onto the disc (1).
Lands reflect the light and pits scatter it, and the sensor detects the difference to read 1s and 0s (1).
